gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Jackery Explorer 500 v2's 6,000-cycle rating ends at 70% remaining capacity while the EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max 500's 3,000 cycles end at 80%. Measured to the same 80% end-point and assuming the battery loses capacity at a steady rate, the Jackery's lead is about 4,000 vs 3,000 cycles (roughly 1.3x), not the 2x the raw numbers suggest.
standout_why: I compared four result pages. powerbencher.com (cited) gives the Explorer 500 v2's '6,000 charge cycles' and says the rating names no capacity end-point, so it can't be compared directly. It never gives the 70% figure and never puts the models on a common basis. powerstations.reviews (cited) lists the RIVER 2 Max 500 at '3,000 to 80%' but has no Jackery 500 v2 or BLUETTI AC50P entry. offgridpick.com gives cycle counts with no 70% or 80% end-point anywhere, and its Jackery entry is the old NMC Explorer 500 at about 500 cycles. The HSN EcoFlow PDF (cited) is an image with no readable text. ChatGPT's own answer sets 6,000 against 3,000 as if they were like-for-like. Rivals cover part of this: one says the figures aren't comparable. None gives the 70% end-point or the adjusted gap.
decides: The Jackery stays the better pick for battery life, but by a smaller margin. Measured to the same 80% point and assuming steady capacity loss, the Explorer 500 v2 gets an estimated 4,000 cycles against EcoFlow's 3,000. Over its whole life it delivers about 2,611 kWh against 1,347 kWh, assuming average capacity is the midpoint between new and end-of-life. For someone using it a few dozen times a year, both batteries outlast any realistic ownership, so the $309 EcoFlow is still the value pick. The extra cycles only justify paying more for the Jackery if it's used every day (solar or daily cycling).

findings.label: Cycle life on a common 80% basis (estimate)
findings.value: Jackery Explorer 500 v2 ≈ 4,000 cycles to 80% vs EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max 500 3,000 cycles to 80%
findings.source_title: How Long Does Jackery Explorer 500 Last? 500 vs 500 v2 Comparison (Jackery UK)
findings.note: My own arithmetic, assuming the battery loses capacity at a steady rate: losing 30% over 6,000 cycles is 0.005% per cycle, so it reaches 80% after 20 / 0.005 = 4,000 cycles. Real LiFePO4 fade is not steady, so treat this as an estimate. Neither maker publishes the Jackery's cycle count to 80%.
